newsitem.title: UK: Britain orders inquiry on PacifiCorp's bid for Energy Group.
newsitem.headline: Britain orders inquiry on PacifiCorp's bid for Energy Group.

text.p: The government Friday ordered an antitrust inquiry into PacifiCorp's planned $6 billion friendly takeover of Energy Group Plc, Britain's biggest electricity distributor.

The move by the new Labour government marked the first time that an American company's takeover of a British electricity company has been sent to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission for investigation.
PacifiCorp, which is based in Portland, Ore., and Energy Group agreed in June to combine into one of the world's biggest energy companies.
Under former Conservative Prime Minister John Major, the government stood by and watched seven of its 12 regional electricity companies taken over by American firms.

However, in a move that sent Energy Group's shares plunging, Trade and Industry Minister Margaret Beckett said Friday that she was concerned enough about the deal to refer it to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.

"The supply, distribution and generation of electricity is of fundamental importance to the UK economy," she said in a statement. "I consider that the merger does raise important regulatory issues that would benefit from a thorough investigation by the MMC."

Energy Group controls electricity giant Eastern Electricity, which was bought in 1995 by the once-mighty industrial conglomerate Hanson. After Hanson's split-up in February, it spun off its U.S.-Australian Peabody Coal unit and Eastern under the name Energy Group.

Beckett said she had not been convinced by arguments put forward by the Office of Fair Trading and electricity regulator Stephen Littlechild, who said that on balance the merger should be cleared subject to assurances from the two companies to address regulatory concerns.

The bid has been dogged by concerns that the deal might be hampered by the Labour government, which has been a fierce critic of the previous government's policy in a wave of takeovers in the electricity sector.
Although Beckett said her general policy continued to be that mergers would be referred on competition grounds, she said regulatory issues would remain of key importance.

"I shall continue to examine mergers on a case by case basis and where, as here, I believe that as part of a wider public interest scrutiny, important regulatory issues are raised, I may decide that a reference is warranted," she said.
